chapter_summary:
In PostgreSQL, the concepts of "users" and "groups" are unified under a single entity called a "role." This elegant design simplifies access management by allowing you to define a role, assign it various attributes (like the ability to log in, create databases, or be a superuser), and then grant it membership to other roles. When a role has the `LOGIN` attribute, it effectively becomes a "user" that can connect to the database. Without `LOGIN`, a role functions more like a traditional group, primarily used to aggregate privileges and assign them to other roles or users. This fundamental understanding is crucial for building a secure and manageable PostgreSQL environment.

To begin managing access, the `CREATE ROLE` command is your primary tool. When you create a role, you can immediately specify its key attributes. For instance, to create a new role named `app_user` that can log in and has a password, you would use `CREATE ROLE app_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'strong_password_here';`. It's paramount to use strong, unique passwords for all roles that have `LOGIN` privileges. Never use easily guessable passwords or reuse passwords across different systems. PostgreSQL 12 supports various password hashing methods, with `SCRAM-SHA-256` being the most secure modern option, offering better protection against brute-force attacks compared to the older `MD5`. When a password is set, PostgreSQL automatically hashes it using the configured default method.

After creating a role, you might need to modify its attributes. The `ALTER ROLE` command allows you to change various aspects of a role. For example, to change `app_user`'s password, you would execute `ALTER ROLE app_user WITH PASSWORD 'new_strong_password';`. You can also disable a role's login capability temporarily using `ALTER ROLE app_user NOLOGIN;` or re-enable it with `ALTER ROLE app_user LOGIN;`. This is particularly useful for locking out compromised accounts or for roles that should only be used as group containers for privileges. Other attributes like `CREATEDB` (can create databases) or `CREATEROLE` (can create other roles) can also be added or removed using `ALTER ROLE`. For example, `ALTER ROLE reporting_admin CREATEDB;` would grant the `reporting_admin` role the ability to create new databases.

When designing your role structure, it's a common mistake to grant the `SUPERUSER` attribute unnecessarily. A superuser bypasses all privilege checks and Row-Level Security policies, making them a significant security risk if compromised. The principle of least privilege dictates that roles should only have the minimum necessary permissions to perform their designated tasks. Instead of creating multiple superusers, create specific roles with only the `CREATEDB` or `CREATEROLE` attributes if those specific administrative capabilities are needed. Another common pitfall is not setting an expiry date for temporary user accounts. The `VALID UNTIL` clause with `CREATE ROLE` or `ALTER ROLE` allows you to specify a timestamp after which the role's password will no longer be valid, forcing a password change or account deactivation. For instance, `CREATE ROLE temp_dev WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'temp_pass' VALID UNTIL '2024-12-31 23:59:59';` creates an account that expires at the end of 2024.

Understanding the difference between `CREATE ROLE` and `CREATE USER` is also important, though largely historical in modern PostgreSQL. `CREATE USER` is simply an alias for `CREATE ROLE WITH LOGIN`. So, `CREATE USER my_user WITH PASSWORD 'secret';` is equivalent to `CREATE ROLE my_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'secret';`. For consistency and clarity, it's generally recommended to use `CREATE ROLE` and explicitly specify the `LOGIN` attribute when you intend for the role to be able to connect to the database. Finally, when a role is no longer needed, it's good practice to remove it using `DROP ROLE role_name;`. Be cautious when dropping roles, as it will also remove any objects owned by that role unless ownership is first transferred using `REASSIGN OWNED BY role_name TO new_owner;` and `DROP OWNED BY role_name;`. Always perform these cleanup steps to avoid orphaned objects and maintain a clean database schema.

screens.title: Understanding PostgreSQL Roles and Users
screens.subtitle: How roles unify users and groups, and how to create, modify, and retire them safely

narration.text: PostgreSQL uses a single concept called a role to represent both users and groups. That means a single object can carry privileges, be a member of other roles, and optionally be allowed to log in. In practice, a role with the LOGIN attribute functions as a user. A role without LOGIN acts like a group to collect privileges. This design simplifies access control, but it also means you must carefully choose attributes when creating or altering roles. In this chapter, you will learn the precise commands to create and modify roles, how to set and rotate passwords securely, how to set temporary access that expires, and the cleanup steps needed before removing a role to avoid orphaned objects. You will also learn common pitfalls, like overusing SUPERUSER, and the recommended alternative attributes such as CREATEDB or CREATEROLE when limited admin rights are required. Finally, we will walk through a practical scenario that creates a group role for a team and a login user that inherits those group privileges. By the end, you will understand the role model, the right S Q L to manage accounts, and the security practices to keep your database tidy and safe. Consider how a role with or without LOGIN changes who can actually connect and why that matters for least privilege.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A single PostgreSQL role can act as a user when given LOGIN, or as a group without LOGIN; manage attributes with CREATE ROLE and ALTER ROLE.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to tell when a PostgreSQL role is acting as a user and when it is a group, create roles with the right attributes, and update those attributes safely. You will also be able to manage passwords and expirations, toggle login capability to lock accounts temporarily, and follow cleanup steps before removing a role. Each objective is practical: you will write CREATE ROLE statements that include LOGIN and PASSWORD when you need a loginable account, use ALTER ROLE to rotate credentials or disable access, and avoid granting SUPERUSER when less powerful attributes will do. For example, you will practice creating a team role that cannot log in and a team member user that belongs to it; the team role groups privileges while the member role holds the login credential. You will also learn to reassign or drop owned objects before dropping a role to avoid orphaned schema objects. These skills reduce security risk and keep database ownership organized. As you study, consider how assigning the smallest required privileges prevents accidental data exposure.

screens.title: Roles: the single identity model
screens.subtitle: Why PostgreSQL combines users and groups into roles

narration.text: Start with the core definition: a role in PostgreSQL is a single object that can represent a user, a group, or a set of privileges. When the role has the LOGIN attribute it behaves as a user and may establish a database connection. Without LOGIN it functions like a group, intended to collect privileges and then grant them to member roles. This unification reduces administrative overhead: instead of juggling separate concepts for users and groups you work with one entity and assign attributes. A concrete example is an analytics team: create analytics_team without LOGIN to be a container for SELECT and CONNECT privileges. Create analyst_john with LOGIN and make them a member of analytics_team; the user logs in using their password and inherits group privileges. A common misconception is thinking roles that look like groups must be able to log in; they should not, unless you need them to hold credentials. Another confusion arises from using CREATE USER versus CREATE ROLE: CREATE USER is an alias that implies LOGIN, but using CREATE ROLE and explicitly adding LOGIN is clearer and future-proof. Key takeaway: design your identity model with role attributes in mind, and prefer descriptive role names for group containers versus individual login roles. How will you split responsibilities between group roles and login roles in your schema?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A PostgreSQL role is a single entity that acts as a user when given LOGIN, otherwise as a group that collects privileges.

content.html:
Core Concept

Role is identity

A role can contain privileges, be member of other roles, and optionally be allowed to connect via the LOGIN attribute.

Role with LOGIN → behaves as a user able to connect.
Role without LOGIN → behaves as a group for privilege aggregation.
CREATE USER is an alias for CREATE ROLE WITH LOGIN; prefer CREATE ROLE for clarity.
Example
analytics_team (no login) + analyst_john (login)
analytics_team holds privileges; analyst_john logs in and inherits them as a member.
Visual callouts
Misconception
Group roles must not be given LOGIN unless they need credentials; doing so mixes responsibilities and increases attack surface.
Key Takeaway

Use non-login roles as privilege containers and separate login roles for individuals to maintain least privilege.

Check
List roles and inspect the LOGIN attribute to confirm which roles can connect.

screens.title: LOGIN attribute: when a role becomes a user
screens.subtitle: How LOGIN and NOLOGIN control connection capability

narration.text: The LOGIN attribute is the switch that determines whether a role can connect to the database. When assigned, the role becomes a login-capable user and must have authentication credentials, typically a password. Without LOGIN, the role cannot establish a session and instead functions as a collection of privileges that other roles can inherit. This distinction supports clearer separation of responsibilities: group roles aggregate privileges, while login roles hold credentials and are used by people or services. For example, create a role analytics_team without LOGIN to grant SELECT on reporting tables. Then create an analyst_john role with LOGIN and a password that is a member of analytics_team; analyst_john connects and uses inherited SELECT rights. One frequent pitfall is granting LOGIN to administrative or group roles, which allows those group accounts to be used for direct connections and increases risk. Another misconception is thinking NOLOGIN means the role has no privileges; NOLOGIN only affects connection capability, not assigned privileges. Key takeaway: use LOGIN only for roles that must authenticate and use NOLOGIN for role containers. Ask yourself: does this role need credentials, or is it just a privilege set?

keyIdea.title: LOGIN matters
keyIdea.text: Assign LOGIN only to roles that require authentication; NOLOGIN makes a role a privilege container without connection capability.

content.html:
Definition

LOGIN vs NOLOGIN

LOGIN gives a role connection capability and requires authentication. NOLOGIN keeps a role as a privilege container only.

Quick examples
CREATE ROLE analyst_john WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '...' → can connect.
CREATE ROLE analytics_team; → cannot connect but can hold privileges.
Misconception
NOLOGIN does not revoke privileges. A NOLOGIN role can still own objects or hold grants; it just cannot authenticate to the server.
Practical check
Action
Use a non-superuser session to attempt psql connection as the role to validate LOGIN behavior.
Key Takeaway

Choose LOGIN only for roles that must authenticate; use NOLOGIN for privilege grouping.

screens.title: Creating roles: CREATE ROLE syntax and examples
screens.subtitle: Practical command patterns for login and non-login roles

narration.text: Creating roles is a routine but security-sensitive task. The CREATE ROLE command accepts attributes such as LOGIN, PASSWORD, VALID UNTIL, CREATEDB, and CREATEROLE. Use explicit attributes so commands remain clear across administrators and automation. For example, creating a login user named app_user looks like this: CREATE ROLE app_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'strong_password_here';. Use CREATE ROLE analytics_team without LOGIN when you want a group role. A concrete practice pattern is to create a group role first, grant it required privileges, then create individual login roles that are members of that group. When writing S Q L, prefer CREATE ROLE and add LOGIN to indicate intent rather than using CREATE USER which is an alias. A common mistake is embedding weak passwords or reusing the same password across roles. Also avoid creating too many roles with overlapping rights; design role names and scopes deliberately. The key takeaway is that CREATE ROLE forms the basis of account management; write clear, attribute-rich commands and verify the created role with role listing. As you practice, ask: does this role need to log in and which privileges does it need to inherit or own?

keyIdea.title: CREATE ROLE
keyIdea.text: Use CREATE ROLE with explicit attributes to define login capability, password, expiry, and privilege flags; prefer clarity over alias commands.

content.html:
Process Flow

CREATE ROLE examples

Create group roles without LOGIN, then create login roles and make them members. Always use strong passwords and explicit attributes.

Code examples
-- Create a group role (no login)
CREATE ROLE analytics_team;

-- Create a login user and add to analytics_team
CREATE ROLE analyst_john WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'YourSecurePassword123!' VALID UNTIL 'YYYY-MM-DD' IN ROLE analytics_team;

-- Create an application user
CREATE ROLE app_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'strong_password_here';
Notes
  • Prefer explicit CREATE ROLE WITH LOGIN rather than relying on CREATE USER aliasing.
  • Use IN ROLE or GRANT to add membership after creation if preferred.
Practical cards
Common mistake
Using weak passwords or reusing passwords across roles increases systemic risk.
Pro tip
Create group roles first, grant privileges once, and add members to avoid duplicate grants.
Key Takeaway

Write clear CREATE ROLE statements with explicit attributes; verify outcomes by listing roles and attributes.

screens.title: Password handling and hashing
screens.subtitle: Why strong passwords and modern hashing matter

narration.text: Passwords for login roles are necessary for authentication and must be managed carefully. PostgreSQL stores passwords using a hash; older systems used MD5, while modern configurations prefer SCRAM-SHA-256 for stronger protection. When you set a password PostgreSQL hashes it using the server's configured method. This means you should choose strong, unique passwords and rely on the more secure hashing methods if available. For practical examples, set a password with CREATE ROLE or ALTER ROLE and prefer a long, random string rather than simple phrases. A common error is assuming that the database stores plaintext or that changing the password is optional after compromise. If an account is suspected compromised, rotate the password immediately and consider using ALTER ROLE to set a new password or NOLOGIN to disable access until you investigate. Another misconception is thinking hashing alone prevents weak passwords from being guessed; it reduces exposure but strong entropy is still required to resist brute-force attacks. The takeaway: use modern hashing like SCRAM-SHA-256 when configured, choose strong passwords, and have a clear rotation and lockout process for suspected compromises. Password handling and hashing means prefer scram-sha-256 hashing, use strong passwords, and rotate or disable accounts when compromise is suspected.. In practical terms, why strong passwords and modern hashing matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Passwords & hashing
keyIdea.text: Prefer SCRAM-SHA-256 hashing, use strong passwords, and rotate or disable accounts when compromise is suspected.

content.html:
Comparison

MD5 vs SCRAM-SHA-256

SCRAM-SHA-256 offers stronger protection than MD5. When available, prefer SCRAM for hashing stored passwords.

Why it matters
Stronger hashing reduces the risk that leaked hashes can be reversed or used for offline attacks.
Practical rule
Always use unique, strong passwords for login roles and rotate them when necessary.
Scenario and response
Compromise response
If a login role is suspected compromised, either ALTER ROLE to set a new password or ALTER ROLE NOLOGIN to lock the account immediately.
Key Takeaway

Hashing is important, but strong password entropy and rotation policies are equally critical.

screens.title: Altering roles: passwords and login toggles
screens.subtitle: Use ALTER ROLE to rotate credentials and disable accounts quickly

narration.text: ALTER ROLE is the command you use to change an existing role's attributes. Common operations include changing a password, enabling or disabling LOGIN, and granting or revoking attributes like CREATEDB. For example, to rotate a password you would run ALTER ROLE app_user WITH PASSWORD 'new_strong_password'; to lock an account temporarily use ALTER ROLE app_user NOLOGIN; and to restore access use ALTER ROLE app_user LOGIN;. These operations are essential when responding to a suspected compromise or when performing scheduled password rotations. One concrete example: after detecting suspicious activity tied to an application account, an administrator can immediately set the role to NOLOGIN to prevent further connections, then rotate the password and re-enable LOGIN when safe. A common misconception is thinking ALTER ROLE NOLOGIN removes privileges; it does not—it only changes the ability to connect. Always confirm changes by listing roles or attempting a controlled connection. The key takeaway is to use ALTER ROLE to manage lifecycle events for user accounts and treat NOLOGIN as an effective temporary lock while you investigate or update credentials. Altering roles: passwords and login toggles means use alter role to change passwords, toggle login/nologin, and adjust role attributes in response to incidents or maintenance.. In practical terms, use alter role to rotate credentials and disable accounts quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ALTER ROLE
keyIdea.text: Use ALTER ROLE to change passwords, toggle LOGIN/NOLOGIN, and adjust role attributes in response to incidents or maintenance.

content.html:
Process Flow

ALTER ROLE examples

ALTER ROLE updates an existing role's attributes without recreating it. Use it for password rotation and temporary locks.

Code examples
-- Rotate a password
ALTER ROLE app_user WITH PASSWORD 'NewSecurePassword456!';

-- Temporarily disable login
ALTER ROLE app_user NOLOGIN;

-- Re-enable login
ALTER ROLE app_user LOGIN;
Cards
Misconception
NOLOGIN is not a permission revocation; privileges remain assigned, only connection capability is removed.
Pro tip
Use NOLOGIN for faster incident containment than immediately rotating passwords in some scenarios.
Key Takeaway

ALTER ROLE is your primary tool for lifecycle and incident management on roles—use it deliberately and verify results.

screens.title: Privilege attributes: CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, SUPERUSER
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right admin rights without over-privileging

narration.text: PostgreSQL exposes several elevated attributes that grant special capabilities. CREATEDB allows a role to create new databases. CREATEROLE allows a role to create, alter, or drop other roles. SUPERUSER bypasses privilege checks and Row-Level Security, granting full control over the server. The principle of least privilege advises granting only the attributes required. For example, a database administrator who should create databases but not manage roles needs CREATEDB but not CREATEROLE or SUPERUSER. A common error is granting SUPERUSER to multiple accounts for convenience; this significantly increases risk because a compromised superuser account can bypass any security control. Another misconception is thinking that CREATEDB or CREATEROLE implies superuser-level privileges; they are narrower and should be used instead of SUPERUSER when appropriate. If you need a role that can create databases and manage roles but should not be able to bypass security, combine CREATEDB and CREATEROLE and avoid SUPERUSER. The takeaway: prefer specific privilege flags over SUPERUSER, and regularly audit who holds elevated attributes. Privilege attributes: CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, SUPERUSER means grant createdb or createrole when needed; avoid superuser unless absolutely necessary due to its broad bypass of security checks.. In practical terms, choosing the right admin rights without over-privileging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Privilege selection
keyIdea.text: Grant CREATEDB or CREATEROLE when needed; avoid SUPERUSER unless absolutely necessary due to its broad bypass of security checks.

content.html:
Comparison

CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, SUPERUSER

Grant narrow privileges when possible. Only use SUPERUSER for tasks that truly require full control.
CREATEDB: allows creating new databases.
CREATEROLE: allows creating and managing roles.
SUPERUSER: bypasses privilege checks and RLS; high risk if compromised.
Practitioner guidance
Best practice
Assign only the minimum attributes needed for a role's responsibilities; review and remove elevated rights regularly.
Common mistake
Granting SUPERUSER for convenience rather than assigning CREATEDB or CREATEROLE as required.
Key Takeaway

Use attribute-specific grants and reserve SUPERUSER for essential platform-level administrative tasks only.

screens.title: Temporary accounts and VALID UNTIL
screens.subtitle: How to give time-limited access with VALID UNTIL

narration.text: VALID UNTIL is a role attribute that sets an expiration timestamp for a role's password, after which the password is no longer valid. This is helpful for temporary contractors, short-lived service accounts, or onboarding tasks where you want automatic expiry. For example, you can create analyst_john with VALID UNTIL set to a date 30 days from now so the password expires automatically and forces a rotation or deactivation. The pattern reduces administrative overhead for temporary access because you do not need to remember to revoke privileges manually later. A common misconception is that VALID UNTIL prevents the role from being used entirely after expiration; it only invalidates the password, so if the role uses alternative authentication or a different credential mechanism, behavior may vary. Another pitfall is not tracking expiry dates; include expirations in operational runbooks and verify them regularly. The practical workflow is: create the role with VALID UNTIL, monitor expiration, then either rotate credentials before expiry or allow expiry and then re-enable access explicitly when needed. The takeaway is to use VALID UNTIL to enforce time-bound access and reduce lingering privileges.

keyIdea.title: VALID UNTIL
keyIdea.text: Use VALID UNTIL to enforce a password expiry timestamp for login roles and automate deactivation of temporary access.

content.html:
Timeline

Using VALID UNTIL for temporary access

Set an expiry date on a role's password to limit access automatically and reduce lingering accounts.

Step 1
Create with expiry
Include VALID UNTIL in CREATE ROLE to set the expiry timestamp at creation time.
Step 2
Monitor expiry
Track expiration dates so you can rotate or re-provision access before it becomes disruptive.
Key Takeaway

VALID UNTIL automates time-bounds for passwords; combine it with runbook monitoring to avoid unexpected outages.

Example
CREATE ROLE analyst_john WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'YourSecurePassword123!' VALID UNTIL 'YYYY-MM-DD';

screens.title: Dropping roles safely: REASSIGN OWNED and DROP OWNED
screens.subtitle: How to remove a role without orphaning objects

narration.text: Removing a role without first cleaning up its owned objects often leaves orphaned objects and broken ownership. The safe procedure is to first reassign or drop objects owned by the role, then remove permissions and finally drop the role. Use REASSIGN OWNED BY old_role TO new_owner; to transfer ownership of objects such as tables and sequences to a different role. Use DROP OWNED BY old_role; to remove all privileges the role holds. Only after these steps should you execute DROP ROLE old_role; to remove the account. A concrete example: before dropping a service account, reassign its owned objects to a maintenance account and then drop owned grants tied to it. A common mistake is running DROP ROLE immediately, which fails or leaves inconsistent ownership. Another misconception is thinking REASSIGN OWNED removes privileges; it only transfers ownership. The key takeaway is to plan deletions: decide the new owner for objects, perform REASSIGN OWNED and DROP OWNED as needed, and then DROP ROLE to avoid schema issues. Always verify with role and object listings after each step to ensure ownership and privileges were updated correctly.

keyIdea.title: Safe removal
keyIdea.text: Reassign or drop objects owned by a role before DROP ROLE to avoid orphaned objects and broken ownership.

content.html:
Process Flow

Reassign, drop, then remove

Plan ownership transfer and privilege removal before dropping the role to keep schema consistent.

Commands
-- Transfer ownership to new_owner
REASSIGN OWNED BY old_role TO new_owner;

-- Remove privileges owned by old_role
DROP OWNED BY old_role;

-- Finally remove the role
DROP ROLE old_role;
Checklist
Step 1
Decide where to move owned objects to avoid losing access to critical schema objects.
Common mistake
Dropping the role first and then discovering orphaned objects that create maintenance overhead.
Key Takeaway

Always reassign or drop owned objects before DROP ROLE and verify ownership after each command.

screens.title: Principle of Least Privilege
screens.subtitle: Avoid unnecessary SUPERUSER privileges and prefer narrow attributes

narration.text: The principle of least privilege is a security best practice that directly applies to role design in PostgreSQL. Grant a role only the attributes it needs, such as CREATEDB or CREATEROLE, instead of giving broad superuser access. Superuser bypasses all privilege checks and row-level security policies, so if a superuser account is compromised it can do anything on the server. A practical approach is to model administrative responsibilities and assign attributes narrowly: give CREATEDB to roles that must create databases, and CREATEROLE to those that must manage accounts. For tasks requiring both, combine the attributes deliberately rather than defaulting to SUPERUSER. A common managerial mistake is creating multiple superusers for convenience; this multiplies risk and makes audits harder. Another misconception is that removing superuser from a role will not affect existing objects the role owns—ownership still remains and requires explicit reassignment if needed. The takeaway is to design role hierarchies where higher privilege is rare and audited. Ask yourself: can this task be done with CREATEDB or CREATEROLE instead of SUPERUSER? Principle of Least Privilege means limit elevated attributes, prefer attribute-specific grants, and audit superuser assignments to reduce risk.. In practical terms, avoid unnecessary superuser privileges and prefer narrow attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least privilege
keyIdea.text: Limit elevated attributes, prefer attribute-specific grants, and audit superuser assignments to reduce risk.

content.html:
Hierarchy

Design roles with minimal privileges

Model responsibilities and grant only the attributes needed. Reserve SUPERUSER for essential platform tasks.

Admin role
Use CREATEDB and CREATEROLE where appropriate; avoid SUPERUSER unless a true platform-level need exists.
Key Takeaway

Design a clear privilege hierarchy and review assignments regularly to enforce least privilege.

Audit tips
Check
Regularly list roles and inspect CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, and SUPERUSER to ensure assignments remain justified.
Common mistake
Granting SUPERUSER for expedience rather than modeling needed capabilities more narrowly.

screens.title: Walkthrough: analytics_team and analyst_john
screens.subtitle: Create a group role, create a member login, verify access, and rotate password

narration.text: Let's walk through the supplied hands-on scenario step by step. First, connect as a superuser. Create a non-login role named analytics_team that will serve as a privilege container. Next, create a login role named analyst_john with a strong temporary password and a VALID UNTIL timestamp set to 30 days from now; create it in role analytics_team so it becomes a member on creation. After creating both roles, verify the setup by listing roles and confirming that analytics_team has no LOGIN and analyst_john has LOGIN and the expiry set. Attempt to connect as analyst_john from a new terminal to confirm authentication works. After verification, you will practice rotating the password by running ALTER ROLE analyst_john WITH PASSWORD and choosing a new secure string. Alternatively, to lock the account immediately use ALTER ROLE analyst_john NOLOGIN before investigating. A common error during this workflow is forgetting to set VALID UNTIL or using a predictable temporary password. The key takeaway: follow the sequence create-group, create-login-in-role, verify connection, then manage lifecycle by rotation or disabling as required. When you perform this lab, double-check membership and expiry values to validate each step.

Hands-on

Analytics team lab

Follow the template to create analytics_team, then analyst_john as a login member with an expiry, verify, and rotate the password.

Starter commands
-- Create the analytics team role (no login)
CREATE ROLE analytics_team;

-- Create a login user and add to analytics_team
CREATE ROLE analyst_john WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'YourSecurePassword123!' VALID UNTIL 'YYYY-MM-DD' IN ROLE analytics_team;

-- Verify roles
\du

-- Rotate analyst_john's password
ALTER ROLE analyst_john WITH PASSWORD 'NewSecurePassword456!';

-- To lock quickly
ALTER ROLE analyst_john NOLOGIN;
Checks and tips
Verify
Confirm analytics_team has NOLOGIN and analyst_john has LOGIN and the correct VALID UNTIL date.
Common mistake
Using weak temporary passwords or forgetting to set VALID UNTIL for temporary users.
Key Takeaway

Follow the create-verify-rotate sequence and use NOLOGIN for quick containment when necessary.

narration.text: These are the core ideas to carry forward. Remember that PostgreSQL uses a unified role model where LOGIN makes a role behave as a user and NOLOGIN makes it a group. CREATE ROLE is the primary command to create both login and non-login roles, and CREATE USER is an alias that implies LOGIN. Use ALTER ROLE to rotate passwords, toggle LOGIN, and adjust attributes. Before dropping a role, reassign or drop owned objects to avoid orphaned schema. Finally, follow the principle of least privilege: prefer CREATEDB and CREATEROLE when specific capabilities are required and avoid granting SUPERUSER unless absolutely necessary. These concepts together form the foundation of safe role and user administration in PostgreSQL. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Three compact concepts to keep in mind when managing PostgreSQL roles and users.

Role vs User
A role with LOGIN is a user; without LOGIN it's a group/privilege container.
Create and Alter
Use CREATE ROLE and ALTER ROLE to set LOGIN, PASSWORD, VALID UNTIL, and privilege attributes.
Cleanup & Privilege Hygiene
Reassign or DROP OWNED before DROP ROLE; prefer narrow attributes over SUPERUSER.
Summary

Treat roles as flexible identities: assign LOGIN only when needed, protect credentials, and remove roles cleanly to maintain a secure and tidy database.

narration.text: Keep these three reminders for daily administration: always use explicit CREATE ROLE attributes when creating accounts, rotate passwords and use NOLOGIN to lock accounts quickly during incidents, and never grant SUPERUSER unless there's a clear, audited need. These practices help prevent privilege creep, make audits straightforward, and reduce the blast radius of a compromised account. Use VALID UNTIL for time-limited access and always run REASSIGN OWNED and DROP OWNED as part of role retirement. Together, these habits keep your PostgreSQL environment secure and maintainable. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Quick Reference

What to Remember

Three compact reminders to apply every time you manage roles.

Create explicitly
Use CREATE ROLE with explicit attributes and strong passwords for login roles.
Contain fast
Use ALTER ROLE NOLOGIN to quickly prevent access while you investigate incidents.
Clean removal
Run REASSIGN OWNED and DROP OWNED before DROP ROLE to avoid orphaned objects.
One-line takeaway

Design roles deliberately, protect credentials, and remove roles cleanly to keep your PostgreSQL environment secure and maintainable.
